MAPLE-Sec: Mobility-Aware Partitioned
Language-Model Engine for Roaming IoT Security
Yuhang Qiu, Member, IEEE, Ziwei Li, Jinfeng Xu, Jialiang Xie, Fangmin Ren, Shirong Guo, Jing Yang, Sunil
Prajapat, and Por Lip Yee, Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract—Mobile Internet-of-Things (IoT) endpoints such as
connected vehicles, wearables, and drones continuously cross
heterogeneous network domains, creating handover-driven attack
surfaces that static, cloud-anchored detectors cannot follow. How-
ever, three obstacles block real-time detection on such roaming
endpoints: detection state is lost at every inter-domain handover;
transmitting raw telemetry to a fixed detector exhausts the
uplink and the device battery; and full-depth language model
inference cannot meet millisecond latency budgets on constrained
hardware. To tackle these challenges, we propose MAPLE-Sec,
a mobility-aware partitioning framework that splits a compact,
security-tuned language model across a roaming device and its
nearest edge node. First, a trajectory-conditioned partition sched-
uler recomputes the split point from predicted handover timing,
residual battery, and uplink quality. Second, a token-budgeted
early-exit mechanism emits a verdict at the shallowest layer
that meets a confidence threshold. Finally, a learned activation-
compression codec migrates the intermediate inference state
across edge nodes during handover without retransmitting raw
telemetry. We formalize the partition-and-migration decision as
an on-device constrained optimization solved in sub-millisecond
time. Extensive experiments across the CIC-IoT and Edge-
IIoTset corpora under both IID and non-IID roaming conditions
demonstrate that MAPLE-Sec sustains detection across mobility
events, improving the converged F1-score by up to 9.3% relative
to Cloud-only and by 2.9 percentage points over the strongest
edge-collaborative baseline (EdgeShard), while reducing end-to-
end latency by up to 2.5×. Ablation confirms that the activation-
compression codec reduces migration energy by 2.4× versus the
raw-activation migration variant.
Index Terms—Mobile IoT security, intrusion detection, large
language models, model partitioning, early exit, mobile edge
computing, handover.
I. INTRODUCTION
Mobile IoT platforms increasingly combine vehicular and
non-terrestrial systems with edge intelligence and distributed

model execution [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. These
systems exchange safety-critical and latency-sensitive data
while moving across heterogeneous network domains, creating
a threat surface that differs from that of stationary networks.
Recent threat-detection studies address smart-city and web
environments [10], [11], but do not consider continuity of
stateful detection across edge handovers.
Recent advances in language-model-based intrusion detec-
tion have demonstrated substantial improvements over clas-
sical signature and shallow machine-learning detectors [12],
[13], [14], [15]. Complementary heterogeneous split and fed-
erated learning frameworks address resource variation during
distributed model training [16], [17], [18]. Security-tuned
encoders can capture semantic behavioral patterns in network
flows, generalizing across attack families that would require
separate classifiers in traditional systems. Edge-collaborative
inference frameworks [19], [20] have further made it practical
to run such models at inference latencies compatible with
mobile workloads, by distributing computation between the
device and a nearby edge node. Mobility-aware offloading
[21], [22], [23] and resource scheduling under handover [24],
[25], [26] have matured into a well-studied sub-field of mobile
edge computing.
Despite these advances, a critical gap remains unaddressed:
none of the existing paradigms accounts for the loss of
inference state at inter-domain handover. When a roaming
endpoint moves from one edge domain to another, any stateful
language-model detector bound to the departing edge node
loses the accumulated behavioral context for that device.
The detection system must either restart from a cold state,
producing a blind spot of several hundred milliseconds to
several seconds, or fall back to a distant cloud anchor at the
cost of prohibitive uplink latency and energy. This handover-
induced detection gap is not a corner case: in the mobility
profile evaluated in this study, handovers occur every 6–12
seconds, so repeated restarts can occupy a non-negligible frac-
tion of the mission. Existing intrusion-detection surveys for
IoT and vehicular networks [27], [28], [29] discuss mobility-
related security challenges but do not provide a mechanism for
migrating intermediate inference state between edge nodes.
Three specific obstacles prevent existing methods from solv-
ing this problem. First, intermediate inference state is bound
to a fixed compute location, making mobility and detection
continuity structurally incompatible without explicit migration
support. Second, even if state were migrated, doing so by
transmitting raw activations or raw telemetry would consume
scarce uplink bandwidth and device battery, both of which
arXiv:2610.37147v1  [cs.NI]  27 Oct 2026


--- Page 2 ---
2
are already degraded at cell edges. Third, running a full-depth
language model on every flow violates the millisecond latency
budgets imposed by mobile IoT applications, particularly on
constrained endpoint hardware.
To
close
this
gap,
this
paper
presents
MAPLE-Sec,
a Mobility-Aware Partitioned Language-model Engine for
Security in roaming IoT networks. MAPLE-Sec partitions a
compact, security-tuned language model between the roaming
device and the nearest edge node, and migrates compressed
intermediate inference state across edge domains during han-
dover. The framework couples three co-designed mecha-
nisms: a trajectory-conditioned partition scheduler (TPS), a
token-budgeted early-exit mechanism (TBEE), and a learned
activation-compression codec (ACC). Their design is directly
motivated by the three obstacles above, and their experimental
gains close the loop back to the original three-challenge
framing. Fig. 1 shows the overall system scenario; Fig. 6
details how each component differs from its na¨ıve counterpart.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows.
1) Novel state-migration mechanism for roaming IoT
security (ACC): MAPLE-Sec introduces, to the best
of our knowledge, the first confidence-gated, rate-
constrained activation-compression codec that migrates
language-model inference state across edge nodes dur-
ing handover. Unlike generic Follow-Me Cloud service
migration [30], [31], which moves service containers
without preserving neural inference context, ACC com-
presses the split activation to 16% of its original size
using a task-informed rate-distortion loss, guaranteeing
that behavioral context survives the handover interval.
2) Mobility-adaptive
partition
scheduling
(TPS): A
trajectory-conditioned partition scheduler recomputes
the device/edge split point at every inference step from
three runtime signals: predicted time-to-handover ˆh,
residual battery b, and uplink quality q. This dynamic
adaptation, absent from all prior static-partition frame-
works [19], [2], [20], reduces migrated payload and
device energy by matching the partition to the current
mobility state rather than fixing it at deployment time.
3) Budget-constrained early exit (TBEE): A token-
budgeted early-exit mechanism terminates inference at
the shallowest layer meeting a calibrated confidence
threshold, with a hard budget that bounds worst-case la-
tency even for adversarially difficult flows. This extends
prior early-exit work [32], [33], [34] with an explicit
budget parameter, providing latency guarantees that prior
confidence-only exit rules cannot deliver.
4) Joint constrained optimization: The three mechanisms
are coupled through a mixed-integer program over la-
tency, energy, and detection confidence, solved in O(L2)
time via enumeration over the small discrete domain.
A bounded-suboptimality proposition (Proposition 1)
quantifies the cost gap as a function of classifier cali-
bration error, providing the first formal optimality guar-
antee for this class of mobility-aware inference control
problems.
5) Comprehensive
empirical
validation: Experiments
on CIC-IoT 2023 and Edge-IIoTset, replayed under a
SUMO/LuST urban mobility trace on a physical Jetson
Orin Nano, show that MAPLE-Sec achieves a 9.3%
relative F1 improvement over the stationary Cloud-only
detector and a 2.9 percentage-point gain over EdgeShard
[2], while reducing end-to-end latency by 2.5×. Ablation
confirms that each module is individually necessary.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec-
tion II presents background and motivating measurements.
Section III surveys related work and identifies the research
gap. Section IV describes the MAPLE-Sec architecture and
its three modules. Section V formulates and solves the
joint optimization. Section VI details the experimental setup.
Section VII reports and interprets performance results. Sec-
tion VIII concludes with directions for future work.
II. BACKGROUND AND MOTIVATION
We motivate MAPLE-Sec with three measurements that
establish the reality of each challenge. All motivating experi-
ments use the same 12-layer security-tuned encoder (L = 12)
and the same CIC-IoT corpus used in the main evaluation
(Section VI), replayed under a 5G NR mobility trace (cell
radius 250 m, UE speed 30–90 km/h, handover every 6–12 s)
generated with SUMO 1.18 on the LuST Luxembourg sce-
nario. Malicious flows are sampled from CIC-IoT and injected
onto the replayed trace at a 20% attack rate.
A. Threat Model
MAPLE-Sec targets roaming IoT endpoints whose traffic
traverses multiple administrative domains. The adversary is
any network entity that injects, replays, or manipulates flows
between the roaming device and the edge node. Concretely,
we assume: (a) the endpoint itself may be compromised and
may inject malicious flows into its own uplink stream; (b)
on-path attackers between the device and the serving edge
node can observe or replay packets; (c) edge nodes are honest-
but-curious: they execute the model tail faithfully but are not
trusted with plaintext behavioral anchors. MAPLE-Sec does
not defend against a fully compromised edge node. The ACC
migration payload zk carries only compressed activations and
anchor scores, not raw traffic; it must be integrity-protected
(e.g., via DTLS or a MAC tag) in transit between edge
nodes to prevent replay attacks during handover. Detection
confidentiality is not required because verdicts are consumed
locally.
B. Handover-Induced Detection Discontinuity
A stateful detector bound to a single compute location
cannot follow a roaming endpoint without interruption. To un-
derstand the magnitude of this effect, we conduct a motivating
experiment in which an endpoint streams a mixed benign and
malicious flow while handing over at t = 6 s. We compare a
static cloud-anchored detector, an edge-pinned detector that
cannot migrate state, and MAPLE-Sec. Fig. 2 shows that
the static detector’s F1-score collapses from 0.94 to below
0.40 around the handover and recovers only slowly, while the
edge-pinned detector permanently loses behavioral context and

“tail” to the nearest edge node. As the endpoint hands over from edge node A to B, the trajectory-conditioned partition scheduler (TPS) recomputes the split
point, the token-budgeted early-exit (TBEE) module returns shallow verdicts for easy flows, and the activation-compression codec (ACC) migrates intermediate
inference state between edge nodes so behavioral context survives the handover.
plateaus near 0.62. These results show that binding inference
state to a fixed location creates prolonged detection blind spots
that accumulate across thousands of handover events, directly
motivating the state-migration approach taken by MAPLE-Sec.
Therefore, it is essential to migrate anchored inference state
across edge nodes as the device moves.
Fig. 2. At handover (t = 6 s), Cloud-only loses 54 F1 points and takes 4 s
to recover; edge-pinned loses behavioral context permanently and plateaus
at 0.62 F1. MAPLE-Sec holds F1 above 0.90 throughout, confirming that
inference-state migration is the key enabler for continuous detection under
mobility.
C. Uplink and Energy Cost Under Motion
Shipping raw telemetry to a fixed detector is wasteful
when the device can summarize locally. To quantify this, we
measure normalized uplink volume and device energy for three
strategies: cloud-only with raw telemetry, edge offload with
raw activations, and MAPLE-Sec with its learned activation
codec. Fig. 3 shows, on a logarithmic scale, that MAPLE-Sec
reduces uplink volume by more than an order of magnitude
relative to cloud-only and roughly 6× relative to raw-activation
offload, with commensurate energy savings. The results reveal
that uncompressed offload squanders the scarce uplink and
battery of a moving device. Therefore, it is paramount to
migrate a compressed representation of inference state rather
than raw telemetry.
Fig. 3.
ACC reduces uplink volume by 6× and device energy by 5.8×
relative to raw-activation offload (log scale), confirming that rate-distortion
compression is the key enabler for practical state migration.


--- Page 4 ---
4
D. Latency-Bounded Inference on Constrained Hardware
Many roaming flows are benign and separable at shallow
depth, yet fixed-depth inference pays the full cost regardless.
We profile per-layer cumulative latency and verdict confidence
for the security encoder. Fig. 4 shows that cumulative latency
grows linearly with depth while verdict confidence saturates
above the threshold τ = 0.90 by the fourth layer for the ma-
jority of flows. This saturation is structural rather than dataset-
specific: the encoder learns shallow discriminative features
that separate benign from attack traffic without requiring full-
depth processing for most flows. Therefore, it is imperative
to terminate inference at the shallowest layer that is confident
enough.
Fig. 4. Per-layer cumulative latency (left axis) and verdict confidence (right
axis). Confidence saturates above τ = 0.90 at layer 4 for the majority of
flows, showing that full-depth inference wastes over half the latency budget
on flows that are already separable at shallow depth.
Challenge-to-module mapping. The three challenges above
map one-to-one onto the three MAPLE-Sec modules intro-
duced in Section IV:
• C1 (detection discontinuity) →ACC, the activation-
compression codec that migrates state across edge nodes
(Sec. IV-E).
• C2
(uplink/energy
cost)
→
TPS,
the
trajectory-
conditioned partition scheduler that minimizes transmit-
ted volume under motion (Sec. IV-C).
• C3 (latency-bounded inference) →TBEE, the token-
budgeted early-exit mechanism (Sec. IV-D).
III. RELATED WORK
A. LLM and Transformer-Based Intrusion Detection
Language-model detectors have rapidly advanced from
proof-of-concept to near-production accuracy for IoT and ve-
hicular intrusion detection. SecurityBERT [14] and IoV-BERT-
IDS [13] fine-tune BERT-class encoders on IoT and V2X
traffic, achieving strong F1 across multiple attack families.
Kheddar [12] surveys transformer and LLM architectures for
intrusion detection across IoT, ICS, and mobile domains,
concluding that language-model detectors consistently out-
perform CNN and LSTM baselines on complex multi-class
traffic. Zhang et al. [15] extend the paradigm to malicious-
traffic detection via prompting and in-context learning, while
the Zero-X framework [35] combines federated learning with
open-set detection for zero-day attacks in IoV. Lai et al. [36]
add a privacy-preserving transformer layer for secure V2X
intrusion detection. Fan et al. [37] propose cloud-edge-vehicle
collaboration for auto-updating IDS in vehicular networks,
and Liu et al. [38] use blockchain and federated learning for
collaborative IDS in vehicular edge computing. Al-Hawawreh
and Hossain [39] adopt federated learning over satellite mesh
networks for autonomous vehicle protection. None of these
works addresses the handover-driven loss of stateful inference
context that MAPLE-Sec targets.
B. Edge Inference and Model Partitioning
Splitting large models between device and edge has received
substantial attention. EdgeLLM [19] accelerates on-device
LLM inference via speculative decoding; EdgeShard [2] shards
LLM layers across multiple edge nodes with static partition-
ing; and Ye et al. [20] explore hybrid model parallelism for
collaborative edge transformer inference. Zhang et al. [40]
analyze edge inference for generative LLMs under wireless
constraints, while Picano et al. [41] model LLM layer de-
ployment across heterogeneous edge networks as a matching
game. Xu et al. [42] study joint inference offloading and model
caching for collaborative small-and-large LLM deployments.
He et al. [43] apply active inference for LLM offloading
and resource allocation at the cloud-edge boundary. Hu et
al. [44] propose a cloud-edge architecture for multimodal
LLM-based driver assistance. Friha et al. [27] survey LLM-
based edge intelligence broadly. All of these works assume
a stationary device-to-edge association; none addresses state
migration during handover.
C. Early-Exit Neural Inference
ClassyNet [32] demonstrates class-aware early-exit net-
works for edge devices, showing that per-sample depth adap-
tation dramatically cuts latency. UCBEE [33] frames the exit
decision as a multi-armed bandit, providing online policies
with regret guarantees. Rahmath et al. [34] survey early-
exit deep networks comprehensively, and Xun et al. [45]
realize early-exit networks on reconfigurable hardware. Ferrag
et al. [28] survey vulnerabilities and defenses for 6G IoT
edge learning. TBEE in MAPLE-Sec extends the early-exit
paradigm with an explicit token budget that guarantees worst-
case exit under mobility-induced latency constraints, a feature
absent from prior works.
D. Mobile Task Offloading Under Mobility
MESON [21] proposes mobility-aware dependent task of-
floading for urban vehicular edge computing, jointly optimiz-
ing execution and migration. Maleki et al. [22] study handover-
enabled dynamic offloading for vehicular MEC. Dai et al. [23]
use meta-reinforcement learning for multi-task offloading in
vehicular edge computing, and Liu et al. [24] optimize task
offloading with dependency guarantees via distributed deep
RL. Li et al. [25] address computation offloading in resource-
constrained MEC, and Yang et al. [26] optimize task offloading
under user satisfaction constraints in C-RAN with MEC. These


--- Page 5 ---
5
works migrate compute tasks but do not migrate inference state
for a neural model serving security verdicts; MAPLE-Sec fills
this gap through ACC.
E. Research Gap and Positioning
Table I maps the capabilities of the three closest 2024–2026
works against MAPLE-Sec. The table reveals that no prior
work simultaneously satisfies all four required properties: (i)
a device-to-edge model partition that adapts to mobility state;
(ii) inference-state migration that preserves behavioral context
across handover; (iii) a latency bound enforced by an early-exit
mechanism with a worst-case budget; and (iv) evaluation under
realistic roaming conditions on mobile-class hardware. LLM-
based IDS works [13], [12], [14] address property (iv) only
under stationary conditions. Model-partitioning works [19],
[2], [20] address property (i) with a static partition, which
is insufficient under mobility. Early-exit works [32], [33],
[34] address property (iii) without the budget enforcement or
the mobility context. Task-offloading works [21], [22], [23]
address mobility-driven computation migration but do not pre-
serve neural inference state. The 2026 works on control-plane
anomaly detection [46], adaptive Wi-Fi IPS [47], and CAV
misbehavior detection [29] address subsets of the problem
but leave the combination unresolved. MAPLE-Sec is the first
framework to close all four gaps jointly through the co-design
of TPS, TBEE, and ACC.
IV. MAPLE-SEC SYSTEM DESIGN
A. System Model
We consider a roaming IoT endpoint and a set of edge nodes
E = {e1, . . . , eM} deployed across administrative domains.
The participating entities are:
• the endpoint, which holds the shallow head of the model
(layers 1..k) and a partition controller;
• the serving edge node em, which executes the tail (layers
k+1..L) and stores migrated state;
• the anchor store, a lightweight cloud service holding the
shared behavioral anchors against which traffic is scored.
The security model is an L-layer encoder f = fL◦· · ·◦f1 with
an early-exit classifier gℓattached at each layer ℓ. A flow x is
embedded and processed layer by layer; the partition point k
determines which layers run on-device. The global objective is
to minimize a weighted sum of end-to-end latency and device
energy subject to a detection-confidence constraint:
min
k, ℓ⋆, µ Ex

λ1T(x)+λ2E(x)

s.t.
Pr[ˆy(x) = y(x)] ≥1−ϵ,
(1)
where T(x) and E(x) are the latency and energy for flow
x, ℓ⋆is the exit layer, µ is the binary migration flag, and
ϵ bounds the detection-error probability. Table II summarizes
the notation.
B. Framework Overview
Fig. 5 shows how the three modules interact. The training
and inference workflow follows three steps: i) the partition
controller queries TPS with the current (ˆh, b, q) to obtain a
split point k; ii) the endpoint executes layers 1..k, and TBEE
checks at each layer whether an early verdict is admissible,
otherwise the compressed activation zk is sent to the serving
edge node for the tail; iii) when a handover is predicted, ACC
migrates zk and the running anchor scores to the next edge
node so inference resumes without restart. The full per-flow
procedure is given in Algorithm 1. Recalling the mapping in
Section II, TPS addresses C2, TBEE addresses C3, and ACC
addresses C1.
C. Trajectory-Conditioned Partition Scheduler (TPS)
TPS resolves C2: it chooses the split point k that minimizes
transmitted volume and energy under motion. The design
rationale is that the optimal split depends on time-to-handover
ˆh, residual battery b, and uplink quality q: when a handover is
imminent or uplink is poor, the device should run more layers
locally to shrink the migrated payload; when battery is scarce,
it should offload earlier. We model the expected device cost
of split k as
J(k | ˆh, b, q) = α cdev(k) + β s(k)
q
+ γ Φ(ˆh, k),
(2)
where cdev(k) is the on-device compute cost of layers 1..k,
s(k) is the size of the activation crossing the split, s(k)/q
approximates uplink time, and Φ(ˆh, k) penalizes splits whose
migrated state cannot be transferred before the predicted
handover. The weights α, β, γ are normalized by b so that
a low battery raises the relative price of on-device compute.
TPS selects k⋆= arg mink J(k | ˆh, b, q) over the discrete
layer set, which is solved exactly by enumeration in O(L).
Remark. Because L is small (tens of layers), the enumer-
ation is trivially cheap and runs between inference steps; the
scheduler reacts to a new handover prediction within one
inference interval.
D. Token-Budgeted Early Exit (TBEE)
TBEE resolves C3: it terminates inference at the shallowest
confident layer. At each layer ℓ, the attached classifier gℓ
produces a verdict distribution pℓand a confidence κℓ=
maxc pℓ(c). Inference exits at
ℓ⋆= min{ℓ: κℓ≥τ ∨Bℓ≤0},
(3)
where τ is the confidence threshold and Bℓis a remaining
token budget decremented by the cost of each layer. The
budget guarantees a worst-case exit even for hard flows,
bounding tail latency. The threshold τ is calibrated on a
validation split to hold the detection-error constraint ϵ in (1).
Complexity. TBEE adds one lightweight classifier evaluation
per layer, an O(1) overhead per layer that is dominated by the
layer’s own compute, and it strictly reduces expected inference
cost relative to fixed-depth execution.
E. Activation-Compression Codec (ACC)
ACC resolves C1: it migrates inference state across edge
nodes during handover without retransmitting raw telemetry.
The codec C : ak 7→zk is a learned encoder/decoder pair

where ˆak = C−1(zk) is the reconstructed activation, g>k

ACC architecture and training. The encoder C is a two-
layer MLP with hidden dimension 128 and ReLU activations;
the decoder C−1 mirrors this structure. For a 12-layer encoder
with hidden size 256, the split activation ak has 256 floats
(1 024 B); the codec bottleneck is 40 floats (160 B), giving
a compression ratio of 6.4× at ρ = 0.05. The codec has
134 K trainable parameters. It is trained jointly with the
encoder head on the CIC-IoT training split for 20 epochs
using Adam with learning rate 10−3. Encode and decode each
take under 0.3 ms on the Jetson Orin Nano (measured via
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW)), contribut-
ing approximately 0.6 ms to the end-to-end 23 ms budget at
k = 6. The migrated payload per flow is 160 B; over a 4 Mb/s
cell-edge uplink this transfer takes 0.32 ms, well within the
6–12 s handover interval.

V. PROBLEM FORMULATION AND SOLUTION
A. Problem Formulation
We make the joint decision in (1) concrete. The decision
variables are:
• k ∈{1, . . . , L}: the device/edge partition point;
• ℓ⋆∈{1, . . . , L}: the per-flow exit layer;
• µ ∈{0, 1}: whether to migrate state at the upcoming
handover.
The end-to-end latency of a flow is
T = tdev(min(ℓ⋆, k))

(5)

E = πc tdev(min(ℓ⋆, k)) + ⊮[ℓ⋆> k] πtx

,
(6)
where πc (W) and πtx (W) are the compute and transmit power
of the endpoint, respectively. The optimization is
min
k,ℓ⋆,µ
λ1T + λ2E

(OC2)

Constraint (OC1) enforces the detection-confidence require-
ment; (OC2) requires that a migrated payload transfer before
the predicted handover; (OC3) caps device energy at the
residual battery budget; (OC4) keeps the split no deeper than
the exit. Problem (7) is a mixed-integer program over a small
discrete domain.
The handover penalty function in (2) is defined as
Φ(ˆh, k) = max

0, s(k)
q
+ tmig −ˆh

,
(8)
which is zero when the payload can be transferred before the
handover and grows linearly with the deficit otherwise. The
behavioral anchor score for a flow x is updated after each
verdict via the exponential moving average
At+1(c) = (1 −αs) At(c) + αs pℓ⋆(c),
(9)
where αs ∈(0, 1) is a smoothing coefficient and pℓ⋆(c) is the
per-class probability at the exit layer. Anchor scores in (9) are
the quantities migrated by ACC alongside zk.
Complexity statement. The feasible domain has size O(L2)
in (k, ℓ⋆) with a binary µ, so the exact optimum is found
by enumeration in O(L2), which for L of a few tens is
microsecond-scale on the endpoint.

EdgeShard is not asymptotic (both are O(Ld2)) but constant-
factor: TBEE exits at layer 4.3 on average (out of 12), cutting
executed layers by 64%, and TPS reduces the uplink payload
from 1 024 B to 160 B. The ACC encode and migrate steps
together add less than 0.6 ms, which is negligible relative to
the 35 ms saved by the early exit.
C. Solution Approach
We decouple (7) into an offline split policy and an online
exit decision. Offline, TPS precomputes, for a grid of (ˆh, b, q),
the split k⋆minimizing the expected objective in (2); this
yields a lookup policy evaluated in O(1) at run time. Online,
TBEE realizes the exit decision ℓ⋆per flow via (3), and the
migration flag µ is set when a handover is predicted within the
tail’s remaining time. The combined controller runs in O(L)
on-device per flow with no iterative solver, satisfying the sub-
millisecond budget.
Convergence and optimality. The online exit rule (3) is
monotone in κℓ: once the threshold is crossed it is never
revoked, so the rule terminates in O(L) steps and returns a
feasible solution to (7) whenever constraint (OC1) is satisfied.
The following proposition formalizes the cost gap incurred
when confidence estimates are imperfect.
Proposition 1 (Bounded suboptimality). Let δ = E[|κℓ−
Pr[ˆy = y|aℓ]|] be the expected calibration error of the per-
layer classifiers, and let L⋆
δ=0 denote the offline-optimal exit
layer under perfect calibration. Then the expected per-flow
cost of the online controller satisfies
E[λ1T +λ2E] ≤E[λ1T ⋆+λ2E⋆]+(λ1cmax +λ2emax) L δ,
(10)
where cmax and emax are the per-layer latency and energy
bounds. The suboptimality gap vanishes as δ →0, and for
the temperature-scaled classifiers used in Section VI the gap
is empirically below 3% of the optimal cost.
Proposition 2 (Detection continuity across handover). Let
∆denote the payload transfer time for zk at the cell-edge
uplink rate qmin, and let ˆh be the predicted time-to-handover.
If ACC is active and constraint (OC2) is satisfied, then the
probability that a handover event produces a detection blind
spot of duration longer than ∆is bounded by
Pr[blind spot > ∆] ≤Pr

ˆh < s(k⋆)
qmin
+ tmig

(11)
which approaches zero as handover prediction accuracy im-
proves. In our SUMO/LuST evaluation, this probability is em-
pirically 0.038, compared to 1.0 for the edge-pinned detector
without state migration.
VI. IMPLEMENTATION AND EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
Hardware and runtime platform. The device head runs on
a physical NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano (8-core Arm Cortex-
A78AE, 8 GB LPDDR5, 15 W TDP) under NVIDIA Linux
for Tegra (L4T) 36.3 (Ubuntu 22.04 base). Inference on the
device head is executed via TensorRT 8.6 with FP16 precision.
The model tail runs on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 edge server
(24 GB VRAM, 64 GB host RAM) under Ubuntu 22.04 and
TensorRT 8.6. The two hosts are connected by a Linux tc


--- Page 9 ---
9
netem link configured to emulate a 5G NR channel: cell-
edge uplink 4 Mb/s with 15 ms RTT and 1% packet loss; mid-
cell 25 Mb/s with 5 ms RTT and 0.1% packet loss. Handover
events are injected by toggling the active tc qdisc every
6 to 12 s according to the SUMO mobility trace described
below. End-to-end latency is measured on the Jetson Orin
Nano using clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW)
bracketing the full inference path from packet arrival to verdict
emission.
Mobility
model. The mobility trace is generated with
SUMO 1.18 on the LuST (Luxembourg SUMO Traffic) sce-
nario, a 400 km2 urban and suburban road network. We extract
1 200 vehicle traces (mean speed 42 km/h, peak 90 km/h).
Each trace drives the tc netem handover schedule and
the predicted time-to-handover ˆh fed to TPS. CIC-IoT and
Edge-IIoTset flows are replayed onto the mobility trace in
temporal order, with malicious flows injected at a 20% rate.
The resulting dataset spans 14 000 handover events across the
two corpora.
Datasets. We evaluate on two public IoT intrusion corpora.
CIC-IoT 2023 [48] contains 33 attack types across 47 feature
classes and approximately 2.9 M flows; we use the 80/10/10
train/val/test split released by the dataset authors. Edge-IIoTset
[49] covers fourteen attack categories over IoT and IIoT
protocols (MQTT, CoAP, Modbus, DNP3) with approximately
1.1 M flows; we use the same 80/10/10 split. Both corpora
are stationary traffic captures; malicious flows are injected
onto the SUMO/LuST mobility trace as described above.
Each corpus is independently partitioned both IID (uniform
attack distribution across the 4 emulated domains) and non-IID
(Dirichlet α = 0.3 attack-class skew per domain). All results
figures report per-corpus performance separately; Figs. 7 and 8
show CIC-IoT results.
Benchmarks. We compare against four representative base-
lines:
• Cloud-only: full-depth detection at a fixed cloud anchor
with raw telemetry upload, the de facto stationary detec-
tor.
• EdgeLLM [19]: on-device speculative LLM inference,
adapted to the detection task with fixed depth.
• EdgeShard [2]: collaborative device/edge sharding of the
model with a static partition.
• Active-Infer [43]: active-inference offloading and re-
source allocation between device and edge, without state
migration.
Hyperparameters. Table IV lists the key settings. Unless
noted, τ = 0.90, λ1 = λ2 = 0.5, and the codec rate weight ρ is
tuned so the migrated payload is ∼16% of the raw activation.
VII. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
A. Evaluation Metrics
We evaluate MAPLE-Sec across four complementary di-
mensions that together cover detection quality, system effi-
ciency, and mobility resilience.
Detection quality. The primary detection metric is the macro-
averaged F1-score computed over all attack classes, reported
as the converged value after 60 s of wall-clock time in each
TABLE IV

5
experiment. We also report precision and recall per class,
and the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve
(AUC-ROC) for binary (benign vs. attack) discrimination.
For multi-class settings we use the one-vs.-rest AUC macro-
average. All quality metrics are computed on the held-out test
split (10% of each corpus) that was never used during training
or validation.
Latency. End-to-end latency is defined as the elapsed time
from packet arrival at the device head to verdict emis-
sion, measured on the physical Jetson Orin Nano using
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW). We report
mean latency, 95th-percentile tail latency (P95), and the frac-
tion of flows that violate the 40 ms application-layer deadline.
Energy and uplink cost. Device energy per flow is measured
via the on-board INA3221 power monitor (POM_5V_IN rail)
sampled at 50 ms and integrated over the inference interval.
Uplink volume per flow is the number of bytes transmitted
from device to edge (either raw telemetry, raw activations, or
compressed zk), reported on a log scale normalized to the
cloud-only baseline.
Mobility resilience. We define the handover recovery time
as the duration from a handover event until F1 returns to
within 5 percentage points of its pre-handover value. A shorter
recovery time indicates better state preservation. We also
report the blind-spot rate: the fraction of handover events
during which no verdict is emitted for more than ∆= 200 ms,
the threshold above which an attacker can inject a detectable
burst undetected.
Throughput. Verdict throughput is measured in verdicts per
second at a fixed pipeline depth, scaling the number of coop-
erating edge nodes from 1 to 32 to characterize coordination
overhead.
B. Superiority of MAPLE-Sec
All experiments are repeated across five random seeds (data
shuffle and model initialization); figures show the mean and
shaded one-standard-deviation bands. Pairwise comparisons


--- Page 10 ---
10
against EdgeShard use a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test; all
reported differences are statistically significant at p < 0.01.
Fig. 7 and Fig. 8 present detection F1 versus wall-clock
time under IID and non-IID partitions. MAPLE-Sec converges
fastest and to the highest F1 in both settings. Specifically,
under IID it reaches 0.962 F1, a 2.9 percentage-point absolute
gain over EdgeShard and a 9.3% relative F1 improvement
over Cloud-only ( 0.962−0.880
0.880
), while converging roughly 1.6×
faster. Under the harder non-IID partition the gap widens:
MAPLE-Sec reaches 0.941 F1 versus 0.892 for EdgeShard.
This is primarily attributed to ACC, which preserves behav-
ioral context across handovers so the detector does not relearn
after each domain change. In contrast, Cloud-only suffers from
handover blind spots and EdgeShard’s static partition stalls
when uplink degrades at cell edges, leading to slower and
lower convergence.
These results close the loop on the three-challenge framing
of Section II. The 9.3% relative F1 gain over Cloud-only
directly quantifies the benefit of resolving C1: in Fig. 2,
Cloud-only loses 54 F1 points during a single handover and
recovers over approximately 4 s; the IID convergence curve
in Fig. 7 shows that, summed over 14 000 handover events,
this repeated recovery cost accounts for nearly all of the F1
gap. The 2.5× latency reduction over EdgeShard reflects the
interplay of C2 and C3: TPS reduces the uplink payload
so that transmission cost no longer dominates end-to-end
time, and TBEE exits at layer 4.3 on average so that tail
compute cost drops proportionally. The non-IID advantage
(0.941 vs. 0.892 for EdgeShard) is attributable to the anchor-
score migration in ACC: anchor scores in (9) capture the per-
domain attack distribution, so migrating them to the next edge
node eliminates the distribution-shift penalty that a cold-start
detector would pay on each domain arrival.
Table V reports the converged detection quality metrics
for all baselines and MAPLE-Sec on both corpora under IID
conditions. MAPLE-Sec achieves the highest F1, precision,
recall, and AUC-ROC on both datasets, with consistent gains
across all metrics. The precision gain over EdgeShard (0.965
vs. 0.941 on CIC-IoT) reflects the reduction in false positives
attributable to the behavioral anchor migration in ACC: mi-
grating anchor scores preserves the per-class prior, reducing
the tendency to misclassify benign post-handover flows as
attacks. The recall gap (0.937 vs. 0.905 on Edge-IIoTset)
reflects the elimination of handover blind spots, during which
the edge-pinned and static-partition detectors miss attacks
entirely.
Fig. 9 traces the converged-F1 versus end-to-end-latency
frontier. MAPLE-Sec dominates the frontier, attaining the
highest F1 at the lowest latency (23 ms), a 2.5× latency
reduction over EdgeShard at higher accuracy. This is attributed
jointly to TBEE, which avoids full-depth inference for easy
flows, and TPS, which keeps the migrated payload small under
motion.
Table VI reports the full latency and energy breakdown
per method. MAPLE-Sec achieves the lowest mean latency
(23 ms), lowest tail latency (38 ms at P95), and zero deadline
violations, while reducing uplink volume to 160 B per flow
and device energy to 17.4 mJ per flow. The blind-spot rate

Fig. 8. Under non-IID domain skew (α = 0.3), the F1 gap between MAPLE-

C. Impact of Residual Battery Budget
Device
energy
is
measured
using
the
Jetson
Orin
Nano on-board INA3221 power monitor via tegrastats
(POM_5V_IN rail), sampled at 50 ms. Fig. 10 reports end-to-
end latency as the residual battery budget varies. MAPLE-Sec
adapts its split point through TPS: at high battery it runs more
layers on-device and migrates a smaller payload, reaching
23 ms; at 20% battery it offloads earlier, trading a modest
latency rise to 41 ms while respecting the energy cap (OC3).
The fixed-split baseline cannot adapt and holds a constant
55 ms regardless of budget. Notably, even at 80% battery the
TPS adaptation still yields a 12 ms latency advantage over the
fixed-split baseline because the dynamic payload reduction
(160 B to 110 B) saves transmission time at every inference
step, not only in the most energy-scarce regime. This confirms
that TPS adapts correctly across the full battery range.
Fig. 10. End-to-end latency versus residual battery budget. TPS adapts the
split point to the energy budget and outperforms the fixed-split baseline across
the full battery range, not only at low battery.
D. Impact of Edge-Node Scale
A verdict is defined as one per-flow detection decision
(benign or attack class). Fig. 11 shows verdict throughput
as the number of cooperating edge nodes grows from 1 to
32 on a base-2 logarithmic x-axis. MAPLE-Sec throughput
scales approximately linearly in the number of nodes (ap-
pearing as an exponential curve on the log x-axis), reaching
19.4k verdicts/s at 32 nodes because ACC migration cost is
small and decoupled from tail compute. EdgeShard scales
sub-linearly (a flattening curve on the log x-axis) as its static
sharding incurs growing coordination overhead. This confirms
that the design scales to dense edge deployments without
coordination overhead.
Fig. 11.
Verdict throughput versus number of cooperating edge nodes.
MAPLE-Sec tracks the linear-ideal trend more closely than EdgeShard.
E. Ablation Study: Design Priority and Tradeoffs
The ablation study is structured to answer the question
posed in the introduction: which of the three challenges (C1
detection discontinuity, C2 uplink/energy cost, C3 latency-
bounded inference) is most damaging when left unaddressed,
and do the modules interact or remain independent? Fig. 12
reports convergence (panel a) and per-variant cost (panel b).
The design-priority order from most to least impactful is
C1 (ACC) > C3 (TBEE) > C2 (TPS).
w/o ACC (raw migrate): addressing C1 is most critical.
Removing ACC and migrating raw activations degrades con-
verged F1 to 0.889, the largest single-module drop in the
study, and raises migration energy by 2.4×. The root cause
is that 38% of handover events fail to complete payload
transfer within the handover window at 4 Mb/s cell-edge
uplink, recreating exactly the detection blind spot described
in Section II. This result closes the loop on Challenge C1: the
F1 degradation magnitude (0.962 −0.889 = 0.073) matches
the gap between MAPLE-Sec and the cold-restart baseline
observed in Fig. 2.
w/o TBEE (full depth): addressing C3 is the second priority.
Forcing full-depth inference inflates latency from 23 ms to

12

47 ms, violating the 40 ms application-layer deadline for 23%
of flows. This confirms the motivation from Fig. 4: the
confidence plateau at layer 4 is not an artifact of the motivation
experiment; it is structural. TBEE’s budget parameter B0 = 8
ensures that even the hardest flows exit no later than layer 8,
bounding worst-case latency at 38 ms.
w/o TPS (fixed split): addressing C2 is the third priority.
Fixing the partition at k = 6 regardless of battery and uplink
raises energy by 1.7× and latency from 23 ms to 39 ms. The
mechanism is that TPS shifts to k = 9 (more on-device layers)
when the uplink degrades below 6 Mb/s, cutting the payload
from 160 B to 80 B. This is a design tradeoff, not a free lunch:
the device-side compute rises, but total energy falls because
πtx ≫πc at cell edges. TPS alone cannot substitute for ACC
(removing both collapses F1 below 0.82), confirming that the
modules are complementary rather than redundant.
Table VII summarizes the quantitative outcomes of the
ablation study across all five metrics. The table makes the
design-priority ordering C1 > C3 > C2 precise: removing
ACC causes the largest F1 drop (7.3 pp) and the highest blind-
spot rate (38.2%), confirming it is the most critical module.
Removing TBEE does not affect F1 but doubles tail latency
and produces 23% deadline violations, confirming its role as
the latency guard. Removing TPS raises energy by 1.7× and
slightly inflates latency but does not degrade detection quality
in isolation; its value becomes apparent only under energy-
scarce conditions or when combined with ACC removal.
F. Hyperparameter Sensitivity
We
evaluate
sensitivity
to
the
three
main
hyperpa-
rameters.
(i)
Confidence
threshold
τ:
sweeping
τ
∈
{0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99} shows that IID F1 peaks at τ =
0.90 (0.962) and degrades gracefully to 0.943 at τ = 0.70
(more early exits, higher error rate) and to 0.958 at τ =
0.99 (fewer exits, higher latency). (ii) Codec rate weight ρ:
sweeping ρ across three orders of magnitude from 10−4 to
10−1 shows that the payload size decreases from 310 B at
ρ = 10−4 to 60 B at ρ = 10−1, with F1 remaining above
0.950 throughout; ρ = 0.05 provides the best latency-accuracy
trade-off. (iii) Trade-off weights λ1, λ2: varying the latency-
energy balance from (1.0, 0.0) to (0.0, 1.0) in steps of 0.1
confirms that MAPLE-Sec outperforms EdgeShard in F1 at
every setting, confirming the insensitivity of MAPLE-Sec to
objective weighting.
Table VIII extends the main comparison to the harder non-
IID partition (α = 0.3 Dirichlet skew), showing that the F1
gaps observed under IID conditions widen under distribution
shift. MAPLE-Sec’s non-IID advantage over EdgeShard grows
from 2.9 pp (IID) to 4.9 pp (non-IID) on CIC-IoT, and from
3.0 pp to 5.3 pp on Edge-IIoTset. This widening is attributable
to the anchor-score migration in ACC: by carrying the per-
domain attack prior to the next edge node, MAPLE-Sec avoids
the cold-start distribution-shift penalty that all non-migrating
baselines incur at each domain boundary.
G. Comparative Analysis with Recent Approaches
We
position
MAPLE-Sec
against
three
recent
2026
detection-and-mitigation approaches that share parts of its
problem setting, summarized in Table I. Prince and Renjith
detect control-plane signaling anomalies in 5G and 6G cores
and, like MAPLE-Sec, partition the model for slice-level
scalability and use language models for explainable detection
on a roaming IoT platform [46]. However, their partitioning
targets core-network scalability rather than the device-to-edge
split, and the model stays anchored in the core, so it does not
address the handover-induced loss of on-device inference state
that MAPLE-Sec resolves through ACC migration. Sharma
et al. propose an adaptive Wi-Fi intrusion prevention system
whose context- and score-aware policy engine enforces real-
time mitigation once an attack is flagged [47]. That design
is complementary to ours on the mitigation side, but it runs
as a fixed-location prevention layer and neither partitions the
detector nor preserves detection continuity as the endpoint
roams across domains. Lone et al. survey machine-learning
misbehavior detection for connected and autonomous vehicles
and explicitly identify compromise during handover and roam-
ing, as well as spatial partitioning of the monitored region, as
open issues [29]. MAPLE-Sec offers a concrete mechanism
for exactly that gap, migrating anchored inference state across
edge nodes so detection survives the handover that the survey
flags as unresolved.
Across the three works, MAPLE-Sec is distinguished by
jointly providing a device-to-edge partition that adapts to
mobility, state migration that preserves detection continuity
across handovers, and latency-bounded inference suitable for
constrained endpoints. The first two properties are absent from
all three recent approaches, and the combination is what allows
MAPLE-Sec to sustain detection under motion rather than
treating mobility as an exception.
VIII. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we have proposed MAPLE-Sec, a mobility-
aware partitioned language-model engine for real-time threat
detection on roaming IoT endpoints, directly addressing the

handover-driven detection gap identified as a key open chal-
lenge in mobile IoT security. We have observed that binding
detection state to a fixed location creates handover-induced
blind spots, and that uncompressed offload and fixed-depth
inference waste the scarce uplink, energy, and latency budgets
of moving devices. To preserve detection continuity, we have
designed an activation-compression codec (ACC) that migrates
inference state across edge nodes; to control uplink and energy
under motion, we have designed a trajectory-conditioned parti-
tion scheduler (TPS); and to meet millisecond latency budgets,
we have designed a token-budgeted early-exit mechanism
(TBEE). Extensive experiments on CIC-IoT and Edge-IIoTset
under realistic SUMO-generated mobility have validated the
effectiveness of MAPLE-Sec, demonstrating a 9.3% relative
F1 improvement over Cloud-only and a 2.9 percentage-point
gain over EdgeShard, with 2.5× lower latency. Ablation shows
that the ACC codec reduces migration energy by 2.4× over
raw activation transfer, with near-linear scaling to dense edge
deployments. A pivotal direction for future research involves
jointly learning the codec and the anchor representation end-
to-end across mobility traces. In parallel, we plan to extend
MAPLE-Sec to multi-endpoint cooperative detection, where
neighboring roaming devices share migrated anchors to de-
fend against coordinated attacks. The broader vision is a
fully distributed, mobility-resilient intrusion detection layer
for heterogeneous wireless IoT infrastructure, where detection
continuity is treated as a first-class design objective alongside
latency and energy, rather than an afterthought to be resolved
by cloud fallback.
MAPLE-Sec has three principal limitations that future work
should address. First, the mobility model is constructed by
replaying stationary traffic captures onto SUMO-generated
vehicular traces; flows are not natively generated on moving
devices, so the statistical interdependence between mobility
state and traffic pattern is approximated rather than measured.
Second, although the device head is executed on a physical
Jetson Orin Nano and the link emulator uses calibrated tc
netem parameters, the edge tail and ACC decoder run on a
desktop GPU; end-to-end system evaluation on a fully em-
bedded edge node (e.g., Jetson AGX Orin) remains as future


--- Page 14 ---
14
work. Third, the ACC codec was compared in the ablation
against raw activation migration but not against quantization-
only baselines (8-bit, 4-bit) or established learned image-
compression codecs; this comparison will be carried out in
our future work. Addressing these limitations will require
natively mobile traffic generation, fully embedded deployment,
and a broader codec comparison study. As a potential future
direction, we are looking forward to extending our method to
improve the performance of various applications, such as large
language models [50], [51], [52], [53] and distributed learning
system [54], [55], [56].
